subject: Is it possible to estimate individual deviation from structual covariance norm

messages.author: 6180ccabbdf86586
messages.subject: Is it possible to estimate individual deviation from structual covariance norm
parts:
Hi, in a recent study (doi: 10.1073/pnas.2023860118) on morphological integration of human brain, the authors divided cortical surface into 308 brain regions and quantified the cortical thickness (CT) for each brain region among participants. Patterns of correlation between two arbitrary brain regions are represented as the regression line from total least square regression. Each individual was scored for their deviation from these norms, between all pairs of cortical regions, through orthogonal residual from the total least square regression. This individual deviation is defined by the authors as Anatomical Imbalance Mapping (AIM).

Fig 1 from the study demonstrating the construction of AIM is attached.

Just like we could estimate patterns of correlation between brain regions through covariance norms of CT data, I think we could likewise use the numerator of the RV and CR coefficient (i.e., trace(S_12 * S21)) to represent covariance norm for two modules of interest. But I would like to ask if it is possible to estimate the magnitude of individual deviation from this norm for shape data, just like the way AIM is constructed for cortical thickness data.

Thank you.

Kieran

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Is it possible to estimate individual deviation from structual covariance norm
parts:
Kieran,

 

While conceptually there is great similarity between a pairwise association (correlation) of two traits, and the association of two sets of variables (PLS), the mathematical details are distinct. I believe the plot you provided is of a bivariate regression. It is straightforward to obtain a regression, and then deviations orthogonal to that covariation direction.

 

For two modules representing multiple variables in each, the procedure would be somewhat different; and I am not convinced that either the CR or RV best address the question. Instead I would use partial least squares regression.  This finds the maximal covariation between two sets of variables, described as linear combinations in both. It is possible to perform PLS, obtain the PLS scores for each set of variables, perform regression of these, and then the orthogonal deviations from this.  One would have to write their own code for this, as I am unaware of an existing procedure for what you are describing.

 

Best,  

 

Dean

parts:
The convention is to use PLS axis 1 only. However, you might first inspect the D matrix from SVD to see just how much additional covariation is captured by subsequent axes (see Rohlf and Corti’s paper on PLS where they do this).

 

I would be hesitant to use ‘PCA-based’ ad-hoc guidelines for ‘how much’ to capture percentage-wise. Variation explained (as in PCA), and covariation described (in PLS) are not at all the same thing.

 

See prior posts on this list for a discussion of that.

Best,

parts:
No, there is technically not a lower limit on the number of variables. This is an input data dimensionality problem. I will need to consider the extent to which this is a ‘user error’ issue or a bug; as what you tried in your ‘plsb’ example was not anticipated by the geomorph team.  I explain below, along with the solution.

 

First, what you did in that example was call a single landmark in each group variables. That is the unanticipated part: one does not typically do such an operation, as it often leads to nonsensical results.  One reason is that landmark-by-landmark interpretations of shape changes are discouraged due to the GPA step (see last week’s Morphmet thread where this came up in another context).  Your example

 

Now, the consequence of this for your example was that the objects being shunted into two.b.pls were 2 x 30, and not 1 x 2 x 30.  Thus, the dimensions were not consistent from your first to second example. That lead to the incorrect result.

 

If you simply do the following, your second example will work correctly:

 

plsb <- two.b.pls(t(proc$rotated[1,,]),t(proc$rotated[5,,])) # 1 landmark per module

 

NOTE: see that I added ‘t’ before each component. That turns these matrices into transposed matrices, so that each specimen is a row with 2 columns of output.  Now the analysis works as intended.

 

I will have to ponder, and consult with the team, as to whether or not this is in fact a bug, or something we need to warn people about.  But regardless, the fix above will cause the analysis to work properly for your special situation.

Best,

 

Dean

No, there is technically not a lower limit on the number of variables. This is an input data dimensionality problem. I will need to consider the extent to which this is a ‘user error’ issue or a bug; as what you tried in your ‘plsb’ example was not anticipated by the geomorph team.  I explain below, along with the solution.

 

First, what you did in that example was call a single landmark in each group variables. That is the unanticipated part: one does not typically do such an operation, as it often leads to nonsensical results.  One reason is that landmark-by-landmark interpretations of shape changes are discouraged due to the GPA step (see last week’s Morphmet thread where this came up in another context).  Your example

 

Now, the consequence of this for your example was that the objects being shunted into two.b.pls were 2 x 30, and not 1 x 2 x 30.  Thus, the dimensions were not consistent from your first to second example. That lead to the incorrect result.

 

If you simply do the following, your second example will work correctly:

 

plsb <- two.b.pls(t(proc$rotated[1,,]),t(proc$rotated[5,,])) # 1 landmark per module

 

NOTE: see that I added ‘t’ before each component. That turns these matrices into transposed matrices, so that each specimen is a row with 2 columns of output.  Now the analysis works as intended.

 

I will have to ponder, and consult with the team, as to whether or not this is in fact a bug, or something we need to warn people about.  But regardless, the fix above will cause the analysis to work properly for your special situation.

Kieran,

 

While conceptually there is great similarity between a pairwise association (correlation) of two traits, and the association of two sets of variables (PLS), the mathematical details are distinct. I believe the plot you provided is of a bivariate regression. It is straightforward to obtain a regression, and then deviations orthogonal to that covariation direction.

 

For two modules representing multiple variables in each, the procedure would be somewhat different; and I am not convinced that either the CR or RV best address the question. Instead I would use partial least squares regression.  This finds the maximal covariation between two sets of variables, described as linear combinations in both. It is possible to perform PLS, obtain the PLS scores for each set of variables, perform regression of these, and then the orthogonal deviations from this.  One would have to write their own code for this, as I am unaware of an existing procedure for what you are describing.
